notes.meaning: God gave these instructions to both Moses the ruler and Aaron the high priest. Aaron and the priests were responsible for teaching the people the difference between what was clean and unclean. By telling Israel which land animals they could eat, God taught them to obey Him in daily life and kept them distinct from the surrounding nations.

To be clean for food, an animal had to meet two clear tests: it had to have a completely divided hoof and it had to chew the cud. Chewing the cud means bringing up swallowed food to chew it a second time. If an animal did not have both features, it could not be eaten.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic notes teach that chewing the cud represents meditating on God's law, while the split hoof represents discerning between good and evil.

notes.meaning: Animals that had only one of the two marks were still unclean. Camels, rock badgers, and rabbits chew their food again or appear to do so, but they do not have fully divided hoofs. God showed His people that partial obedience or having only half the needed signs was not enough.

The pig has a divided hoof, but because it does not chew the cud, it was completely unclean for Israel. God strictly forbade them to eat pork or even touch the dead body of a pig. This rule kept them from the unwholesome foods and pagan worship habits of their neighbors.

Water creatures were clean to eat only if they had both fins and scales, whether they lived in the seas or in fresh streams. This simple rule provided the people with healthy food while keeping the law easy to understand.

Any water creature without fins and scales was declared detestable. This included creatures like eels and shellfish, which the Israelites were forbidden to eat or touch when dead. Calling these creatures an abomination trained God's people to keep a strong distaste for whatever God ruled out.

God gave a specific list of birds that were detestable and never to be eaten. The list begins with large birds of prey like eagles, vultures, and kites. Because these birds feed on dead bodies and live by bloodshed, they were unfitting food for God's holy people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that birds of prey were declared unclean primarily because they ingest blood and undrained meat from carrion, which the law strictly forbade Israelites to consume.

notes.meaning: The prohibition extended to every kind of raven, as well as ostriches, owls, and hawks. These birds are known for eating decaying meat, hunting violently, or crying out in lonely desert ruins. God warned His people away from animals associated with darkness, violence, and decay.

God also banned water birds like pelicans and cormorants, various species of owls, storks, herons, hoopoes, and bats. Many of these feed on impure marsh creatures, and the bat flies only in darkness. Any bird not on this forbidden list was permitted as clean food.

Flying insects that crawl along the ground on four or more legs were forbidden as detestable. Having wings to fly while creeping in the dust made them unfitting for Israel's table. This taught the people to avoid a lifestyle dragged down by worldly habits.

God made an exception for flying insects that have large, jointed legs for hopping off the ground. Various kinds of locusts, crickets, and grasshoppers were permitted as clean food. These insects provided clean nourishment in the desert and were later eaten by John the Baptist.
All other flying, creeping insects were detestable and could not be eaten. God clearly marked the boundary so the people would not guess or invent their own rules about what was pure.

Touching the dead body of any unclean creature made an Israelite ceremonially unclean until evening. Ceremonial uncleanness was a temporary state that kept someone away from the tabernacle and fellowship with others. The limit lasting only until sunset reminded them that God always provides a way to restore fellowship.
